reading.body:
Frontier AI systems are shifting from text generation toward autonomous agents that control computers, robots, and physical infrastructure, creating safety and security risks that text-only models did not require.

The capability leap is qualitative. Earlier AI models answered questions. These systems make decisions and execute them: controlling browsers and desktops, writing and running code with full codebase access, operating humanoid robots in factories and homes, automating software engineering workflows. The risk profile changes fundamentally when an AI system can take actions in the world or in critical systems rather than merely proposing them. A language model's mistakes are bounded by a user's choice to act on them. An autonomous agent's mistakes execute immediately.

The concentration of these capabilities in US vendors is notable. Six of eight systems listed operate under US jurisdiction, with only Mistral Large 2 built explicitly for GDPR compliance and European sovereignty. This matters because autonomous agents operating across borders or handling European data face different regulatory pressure than text generation tools. The emergence of robots optimized for factory and household tasks adds a physical safety dimension that cloud-hosted models did not face.

The data does not cover deployment scale, energy consumption of these systems, the computational requirements for real-time autonomous operation, or how many data centers these agents will require. It also does not track incident rates or security breaches. What it shows is the category boundary itself: the frontier is no longer capability, but agency.
